name: Hana Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Henri and I milk seventy cows at Les Prés, the farm my grandfather started. We have grass for the cows and twenty hectares of wheat. I'm in the parlour at half five, then feeding calves, and Henri does most of the tractor work. Sunday mornings the cows are milked early so we can be at church by ten.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the calves and I love a quiet parlour, with the radio on. What wears me down is the milk price and the forms. The milk buyer wants everything online now, and I do it on paper first and Henri types it in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we were right not to rush into it. People forget that the cows don't care about computers. I'd say that after church, to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same struggle as ever. My grandfather milked these cows by hand, and I milk them in a parlour, and neither of us ever got a fair price. The milk price went down again in spring, and we've maybe three months put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on milking, same as now. I'd hold off on the new bulk tank Henri wants and make the old one last another year. And I'd keep putting a little in the church fund, because that's not something we cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Thankful, but the milk cheque is still the milk cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the milk price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big supermarkets and the big dairy companies, who squeeze farmers and call it competition. I believe in a free market, but that's not a free market, that's a few giants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anyone want to take on the farm after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Luc works at the feed merchant's office in town. He says maybe one day, which means no. That sits with me more than any computer.

say: We were right **not to rush** into AI.
The **cows don't care** about computers, as she'd say after church.
think: It's the same **milk price** struggle her family has always had.
They have about **three months** saved, and the spring price fell again.
do: Carry on **milking** the seventy cows as now.
Make the **old bulk tank** last another year.
Keep giving to the **church fund** without cuts.
feel: **Thankful**, but the **milk cheque** still worries her.
S0.quote: My grandfather milked these cows by hand, and I milk them in a parlour, and neither of us ever got a fair price.
fieldNote: Her worry is old: the **milk price** and a farm with no clear **successor**.
Free-market in principle, but blames **supermarkets and giants** for unfair prices.
Faith and **church** set the rhythm of her week.

steps.text: Keep milking the seventy cows as now
Make the old bulk tank last another year instead of replacing it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the farm will be the last place to change, and thank God for that. The offices can have their gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means more of the forms go onto computers, and the milk buyer will expect us to use their app. I've never typed a question into a computer and I don't intend to start at fifty-eight. Henri will grumble and do it, or our daughter-in-law Anna will help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Anna to set up whatever the milk buyer wants, and pay her in Sunday dinners. I'd keep the cows and the parlour exactly as they are. And I'd tell Luc to keep his head down at work, because his office is exactly where this lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for Luc more than for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Luc at the feed merchant's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luc does orders and invoices, and if a computer can do that, they won't need three of him. He'd be one of the ones at risk. Maybe then he'd come home, but I wouldn't wish it on him that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try one of these tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Henri says I'm stubborn, and he's right. I'd rather pay Anna in roast lamb than learn it.

say: The farm will be the **last place** to change, and thank God for that.
The **offices** in town can keep their gadgets and their screens.
think: More **forms** go online, and the milk buyer pushes its **app**.
She'll never type questions into a computer, so Henri or **Anna** will.
do: Ask daughter-in-law **Anna** to set up the milk buyer's app.
Keep the **cows and parlour** exactly as they are.
Warn **Luc** that his office job is at risk.
S1.quote: I've never typed a question into a computer and I don't intend to start at fifty-eight.
fieldNote: Firmly **resistant**: leans on family for any screen work.
Her real worry in Steady Disruption is **Luc's office job**.
A hope she won't say aloud: that losing his job might bring Luc **home**.

steps.text: Ask daughter-in-law Anna to set up the milk buyer's app
Keep the cows and parlour running exactly as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the country has lost its head, and that people should look after their own: family, church and neighbours. I wouldn't ask the government for handouts, but I'd say the big companies need stopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm frightened for the farm. Luc's office job goes in 2028, and then by 2031 the big dairies have robots milking thousands of cows. If a robot dairy can sell milk cheaper than my seventy cows can make it, my grandfather's farm ends with me. I'd be sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything to the bone: no holiday, no new tank, the car kept going. I'd talk with Henri about selling the herd in 2030, before the price collapses, and keeping the land to rent out for grazing. And I'd tell Luc and Anna to come and live in the farmhouse annex if they need to, to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and sad in my bones. I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes three years before the robots. What does that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Luc is hit first and we're hit second. The cows still need me until 2031, so I'd have three years to decide whether to sell before the price falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family and the church, before anyone else. Father Michel and the parish would help, and Henri's brother has always said there's room on his farm.

say: The country has **lost its head**; people should look after their own.
No **handouts**, but the **big companies** need stopping.
think: Luc's job goes in **2028**, then robot dairies arrive by **2031**.
Cheap robot milk would end her **grandfather's farm** with her.
do: Cut **everything** but essentials: no holiday, no tank, keep the car.
Sell the **herd in 2030** and rent out the land for grazing.
Offer **Luc and Anna** the farmhouse annex to save rent.
feel: **Frightened** and deeply **sad**; she'd be praying a lot.
S2.quote: If a robot dairy can sell milk cheaper than my seventy cows can make it, my grandfather's farm ends with me.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** hits her son first and the herd second.
Expects to **lose the milk income** and plans to sell the herd.
Leans on **family and parish**, refusing government handouts.
The deepest loss for her is **legacy**, not just money.

steps.text: Cut spending to essentials and drop the new bulk tank
Sell the seventy cows in 2030 and rent out the grazing
Offer Luc and Anna the farmhouse annex rent-free

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for families to plan, and families should be the ones doing it, not the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I can sit my son Luc down and ask him straight whether he wants the farm. The robots would come in 2034, when I'm sixty-six. Either he takes it on and changes it his way, or we sell up properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have that talk with Luc this Christmas, at the table, with Henri there. I'd put a bit more aside each month from the milk cheque. If Luc said yes, I'd let him bring in whatever machines he wanted, even though I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's room to breathe. Five years is a few calvings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd let Luc bring in robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's his farm, it's his choice. My grandfather hated the milking machine too. I'd stay out of the parlour and keep to the calves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if Luc says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we sell the herd in good time, keep the house, and I'll cry for a week. That's the honest answer.

say: Five years is **enough** for families to **plan** what comes next.
Families, not the **state**, should be the ones doing that planning.
think: She can ask her son **Luc** straight whether he wants the farm.
Robots in **2034** come at sixty-six: Luc's way, or **sell up** properly.
do: Have **the talk** with Luc and Henri this Christmas.
Put a bit **more aside** from each milk cheque.
Let Luc bring in **machines** if he takes over.
S3.quote: With five years I can sit my son Luc down and ask him straight whether he wants the farm.
fieldNote: Five years turns fear into a **family decision** about succession.
Her **milk income** is still at risk, so she stays anxious.
Would accept robots only as **Luc's choice**, as her grandfather accepted machines.

steps.text: Ask Luc at Christmas whether he wants to take over the farm
Put more aside from each milk cheque
Sell the herd in good time if Luc says no

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the Lord knows what will happen by then. People should keep working and stop fretting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us, it's mostly beyond our time. I'll be sixty-eight in 2036 and seventy-one when the robots come. I'll be in church giving thanks that the cows outlived the robots on our farm, at least while Henri and I are here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep milking until we stop, maybe at sixty-five. Hand over to Luc if he wants it, or sell the herd. Nothing new this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in the normal way: the milk price, the weather, Luc. Not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this one that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandchildren. Little Marie is nine, and I don't know what she'll do for work. I'd want her to learn a trade with her hands, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my granddaughter Marie that people will always need someone they can trust, and to be that person.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and only the Lord knows what happens.
think: She'd be **seventy-one** when the robots arrive, well beyond her working time on the farm.
The **milk price** stays her everyday worry.
do: Keep **milking** until stopping at about sixty-five.
Hand over to **Luc** or sell the herd.
feel: **Uneasy** in the normal way: **milk price**, weather and Luc.
S4.quote: I'll be in church giving thanks that the cows outlived the robots on our farm, at least while Henri and I are here.
fieldNote: A decade puts robots **past her working life**.
Background worries about the **milk price** keep her uneasy, not calm.
Hopes her granddaughter learns a **trade** with her hands.

steps.text: Keep milking the herd until stopping around sixty-five
Hand Les Prés to Luc or sell the herd when they stop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Luc's job and our milk price both fall inside three years, and we'd have no time to decide properly. What would help is fair milk prices, with the supermarkets kept in check, and an apprenticeship for Luc in something real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. It's what keeps me steady when the milk price is bad, and it would keep me steady through this. A farm is a family, not a business plan, and robots don't understand that.

headlineQuote: A farm is a family, not a business plan, and robots don't understand that.
portrait: Hana, **58**, milks seventy cows on her **grandfather's farm** with her husband Henri.
She has **never used AI** and leaves screen work to Henri or her daughter-in-law.
Her steady worries are the **milk price** and whether her son Luc will take over.
In fast AGI she fears losing the herd and the **family legacy**, and leans on church and family.
With time, she turns it into a **family decision** and refuses handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with her son's job and the milk **price** falling within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair milk prices**, with the supermarkets kept in check.
A real **apprenticeship** for her son Luc.
